speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, June 4, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) made some adverse comment on the price ceiling which the minister had applied, criticizing it considerably. In the course of his remarks he involved social credit ideas and myself. When the minister answered him, he also involved our ideas and myself. At about fifteen minutes to eleven o'clock I rose and made such comments as I had time to make in defence of our views. I think it fitting that I say a little more this afternoon.
The belief was expressed by the minister and by the leader of the opposition that my group were not in favour of taxation or borrowing. I should like to place our position squarely and fairly before the members of the committee.
I did not say that we could carry on this war without borrowing and without taxation, and I have never said that. There is an error on page 3090 of Hansard which I think I should correct before it goes any further. It was probably due to a slip in my language. In answering the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) I am reported as saying:
I did not say I would not tax. I said, "without additional borrowing."
That should be, "without additional debt." Hon. members will find that that is exactly what I had said; I was just repeating. What I did say was that the new money could be got without debt or taxation. .

War Appropriation-Finance

I said that social credit proposes to use the national credit to provide money without additional debt, without additional taxation. That puts an entirely different meaning on the expression used. Hon. members will find that my interpretation is correct. I can understand how the minister interpreted it as he did, but he will find that that is the meaning. In the same passage as reported on page 68 of Hansard of November 13, 1940, I went on to say:
Social Crediters maintain that in any well-organized and well-managed state with rich and varied resources, such as we have in Canada, the national credit can and should be used to provide fair prices and adequate home markets for all essential industries.
There are other passages which I believe ought to be read in this connection. I am doing this in order that the minister may realize that we are not so widely at variance in some respects. It is well that men do not misunderstand each other; in a time like this we need all the cooperation we can get. On page 70 of that same Hansard I quoted the remarks of Professor A. F. W. Plumptre, as they appeared in the October 5, 1940, Financial Post. I quote these words:
The government can always "get money" because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even to taxation, create the required funds. This it can easily do nowadays through the leadership of the central bank and the cooperation of the chartered banks. In this way 200 millions were created in this fashion last autumn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The amendment of the Social Credit party to the resolution reads-Hansard, 1940, page 68:
And this house further regrets the failure of the government to adopt a monetary policy that would permit a maximum war effort without either increasing debt or reducing the standards of living below that necessary for maintaining maximum efficiency.
Does that not indicate that at that time the policy of my hon. friend's party was to conduct the war effort without increasing debt?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister's observation is quite logical, and it will require some explanation in order to make clear the meaning. May I just use an illustration to show the minister that that is not the exact interpretation that should be placed on the amendment. The minister will understand that if he had used the national credit to ' give the western farmer, we will say SI.15 a bushel for his wheat, the western farmer would have been able to buy a great deal more. He would have bought more goods, which would have yielded the government
[Mr. Blackmore.l
more income from taxation, from the tariff and from other means. He would have been better able to pay taxes to his own province, and he would have been in a better psoition to pay his machinery debts, his grocery debts and his other debts. In this way if the income of the people throughout the country were improved, as the amendment clearly indicates the social crediters conceive it should be improved, then the country would move progressively out of debt. It is not easy in a short time to explain in detail this matter to the minister. In the minds of social crediters it is perfectly feasible. [DOT] The minister knows, without looking the matter up, that by refunding debts, he has paid off vast sums of money on the national debt in Canada while the war has been going on. He has paid those debts with more money which he has collected by taxation, and money that he has borrowed. If he had been using the technique of creating money, as far as he could do so safely, he would have been able to pay more of these debts with such money. I am sure he would have found out in other ways, as the great billion dollar gift which we made to Britain will indicate, if carefully studied and fully understood and interpreted, that the debt of the country could be progressively decreased while the war is going on without in any way interfering with the progress of the war. Whether we should be able to get through this titanic conflict with less debt than we started with, even under a social credit technique, I cannot just tell, but I should be quite sure that the debt would be far less than it will be under the system which the minister is following. Do I answer the minister sufficiently?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
He goes on to say:
that is borrowing which creates additional money in the process.
That, from the bankers' point of view, is the way to do it. From the social crediters' point of view new money should not be borrowed. If the money can be created, social crediters urge it is a real asset to the state and should be regarded as such and be a clear addition to the revenues of the state to the extent that that creation can be carried on without causing inflation.
I endeavoured to illustrate to the leader of the opposition this power to create money by reference to the $26,000,000 which were created definitely in the last war by the Department of Finance under the Finance Act of 1914. This amount of $26,000,000 was used definitely for carrying on government business, probably paying expenses of the Canadian National Railways and other busi-44561-1961
ness just as ordinary revenue would be used. Those $26,000,000 were bills, from the printing
press.
Social credit, as its name implies, deals with credit. It conceives that most of the money that is created should be created not as bills but as credit; only enough bills should be created to facilitate the ordinary hand-to-hand business of the country in carrying on its affairs. I want to point out to the leader of the opposition that created money is sound. I do not know whether he knows this or not, but he does not act as though he understood it. As reported in Hansard at page 3080 he spoke in a somewhat disparaging way of the idea of creating money. This is what he said:
This is not fiat money, I would have the hon. member for Lethbridge understand. This is not printing-press money. This is real, good, hard cash paid by the taxpayers of Canada, and it is going to be paid to certain persons.
The leader of the opposition seems to think that money which was created by the state could not be real, good, hard cash. If the leader of the opposition thinks that, he is completely in error.
I wish to go on with several other matters. I believe I have made quite clear the social credit concept; if I have not, I would appreciate it if the minister would ask me questions. The social credit concept is that in any country of rich resources there can be created a certain amount of money depending upon the goods-and-services-producing-and-consum-ing-power of the country. Either that money can be created by the banking system as a debt and be borrowed by the government, or it can be created by the government as a sheer asset of the state, as the quotation I read last night from Vickers' "Economic Tribulation" clearly shows the writer believed. *
May I read a passage from another source which perhaps has escaped the minister's attention. This passage comes from the London Times of recent date and is quoted by the Montreal Daily Herald of June 4 in an editorial, "Will Protective Tariffs Disappear?" I am going to read the words from the editorial. I said last night, rather sternly I believe, that all progressive men everywhere are beginning to see the possibility of creating money. This passage will help to show that even the very orthodox and conservative London Times is beginning to see that possibility. The words are:
We are not likely to solve our post-war problems unless we make up our minds to treat money as a bookkeeping technique to facilitate the production and exchange of goods and services, not as something the supply of which sets a fixed upper limit to our productive activities.
War Appropriation-Finance

May I digress for a moment to point this out. Social credit, as I will develop it if my time permits, conceives that the credit of the state may be used greatly to increase the productive capacity and production of the state-which is an idea that is conveyed definitely by the words I have just read. To continue the quotation:
It plays much the same part in the economic life as railway tickets play in transportation. It is dishonesty, akin to inflation, to issue tickets for more trains than can be run. It is absurd to cut down the railway service because the ticket office has run short of tickets.
That is precisely the concept of social credit.
When we were talking in 1939 there was a vast amount of productive capacity and actual production in Canada which was not being used. We could have created enough tickets, enough money to have caused these productive capacities to come into use and all of these idle goods to be used. As an illustration of what might have been done, just think of the lumber which we were not having very much use for during six, eight or ten months; imagine what would have been achieved by means of a credit expansion which would have resulted in houses being built all over Canada and would have kept the lumber mills busy nine months of that year before they were brought into operation by the demand of war. What a change there would have been in the social conditions among the Canadian people! How much stronger we would have been to fight the war! Such credit expansion would have been an example of tickets created for the goods that were already in Canadian lumber yards-not enough tickets to bring about a scarcity of goods, but merely to stimulate, to motivate production to the highest degree possible. If at any time I do not make myself clear, I shall appreciate it if the minister will let me know.
I have never advocated a limitless creation of money. I hope that never again in this house will the minister or the leader of the opposition or anyone else accuse us even by implication of advocating any such thing. It was the favourite device of Mr. Dunning to say that sort of thing, apparently side-stepping the issue and getting people off on the wrong track. But that is not fair; it is not in the interests of the country. Reference was made last night in two places to unlimited creation of money. As reported at page 3077 of Hansard the minister used these words:
Sounder than the creation of unlimited sums of new money.
We have never advocated that, under any circumstances anywhere since we came to the house. Again as reported at page 3078 he spoke
[Mr. BlackmoreJ
of "the unlimited creation of money." That is a misinterpretation of our ideas. This is the rule:	The amount of money that can be
created and used, as I have said over and over again, depends upon the goods-and-ser-vices producing-and-consuming power of the state. That is the simplest way in which it can be expressed in general terms. It is a fairly accurate way of determining the amount of money that can be created and used. The minister himself has that concept; only he has not our concept of "creating" money; he has the concept of the degree to which the "banks" can create money without causing inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
May I say this for the
sake of clarification. The hon. gentleman seems to argue part of the time that we should run the banks. That is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation policy. He seems to object to the private banking system. Instead of allowing the banks a profit on the carrying on of banking activities, he suggests that the government should carry them on; and, as presumably he would say, that the government should have the profit themselves. Is that the position of social credit?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No; that is not quite correct. The social credit movement believes that the banks can work for the government. The banks do not necessarily belong to the government. It may be quite all right for the government to buy the whole banking system. We would certainly never favour having the government seize it or cause any harm to the bankers. We do believe in private enterprise. That, the minister will find, is the distinctive difference between our movement and the socialistic movement, which seems to favour government ownership and direction. We believe it is better for the country to have private ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I may become, I am afraid, a minister who delays his own estimates, but I should like to ask the hon. gentleman this question. If the private banks, the commercial banks, are to continue in private hands and continue lending money, are they not creating money in the sense which the hon. gentleman implies, and therefore perpetuating what he says should not be allowed to continue? Bear in mind that the hon. gentleman said a few minutes ago that the creation of money should be a state activity, that money is an asset to the country and should be created by the state. Is that position consistent with the position that the private banking system should be allowed to continue?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
First, let me put it
in this way. The Bank of Canada prints bills

War Appropriation-Finance
to-day, and the government theoretically borrows those bills from the Bank of Canada, thereby creating a debt to the Bank of Canada, which is a debt to the government itself inasmuch as the Bank of Canada is a government institution, a branch of the minister's own department, as I understand. In that respect, the government can obtain bills and perhaps credit at a very low rate. It should be able to obtain it at cost of printing, cost of bookkeeping and cost of management.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What about cost of interest
on deposits?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We shall come to
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is part of the costs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I was dealing first of all with the central bank.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I make no pretence at being able to follow the hon. gentleman all the way through, but one thing strikes me. How will you control the issuing of currency or tickets when your productive capacity is in the hands of private enterprise, when it is in someone else's hands and someone else controls it? On what are you going to base the issuing of currency?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not want to keep anyone from asking any questions, and perhaps the minister will allow me to answer the hon. member's question first. It would be better, however, if all questions could be deferred until I get through.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I asked only one question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It would be better if the hon. member would bring that up at the end, because to answer the minister's searching questions is enough for any hon. member, if the situation is to be made clear for the record.- Perhaps my hon. friend will bring it up later.
Answering the minister's question, I would point out in the first place that I was dealing with the central banking function, and theoretically the primary business of the central bank is not paying interest on deposits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When you come to the second ary or chartered banks you are dealing with another problem. The chartered bank has to pay interest on deposits. This causes the private or chartered bank to incur definite costs. Perhaps it costs them 3 per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They pay only one and a half.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I said "perhaps", for the reason that there is a good deal of discussion about the matter. If hon. members will read the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of 1939, they will see how difficult the question was then, and we in this house can hardly hope to settle it if that committee were unable to. But take 3 per cent as the rate and assume that it costs the Bank of Montreal 3 per cent to lend money to the people, taking into consideration what it pays for its own deposits. The social credit position would be something like this. Farmers are producing the very sinews of war, such as milk, honey, beef, wool and so on, and surely they should never be called upon to pay 6 and 7 per cent. That is adding to their costs; it is adding to the costs both to the community and to the government. It is unsound. Social credit would say that probably 2 per cent or even less is all that the farmer should ever have to pay for production loans. The question would be raised, how would the difference be made up to the bank? How would the bank of Montreal be saved from loss?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It would be the difference between three and two.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, a loss of one per cent. I think it will come to be realized as the years go by that the people can afford to have the government subsidize the bank on that loan. If it costs the bank 3 per cent and the government wants the farmer to have it at 2 per cent, the government can afford to pay the 1 per cent; that is, provided the loan is for bona fide production. The increased business will rapidly increase the profits of the bank, which again is an important item. The minister as he realizes has opened up a highly technical question. That is perfectly all right, but it is one which it is difficult to deal with on the floor of the house, one which could be much better dealt with in the banking and commerce committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is an additional subsidy for agriculture; that is all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is nothing very difficult about that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is true. But it is a new idea that I find people do not apprehend quickly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are familiar with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister has
raised an important point After all is said and done, if the production of wool, which is

War Appropriation-Finance
disturbing people greatly to-day in Canada, is so vital to the welfare of Canada, why should the producers of wool be penalized by high interest rates? Looked at logically it never can be sound economics.
I think I have said enough on that point. If the minister has no further questions, I shall now turn aside to deal with the question of the hon. member for Cape Breton South before we lose track of him. The hon. member asked in effect: If the government creates through the Bank of Canada a one dollar bill which gives a claim to a bushel of wheat, how can the government create the one dollar bill giving that claim when the government does not possess the bushel of wheat?
Well, the bank of Montreal and every other chartered bank in Canada were doing that thing for scores of years. They were able to do it; they are able to do it now. When the dominion government created a one dollar bill under the Finance Act of 1914 the dominion did it; they do it now through the Bank of Canada, and that bill is a claim to a dollar's worth of fish, or a dollar's worth of coal-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then there is no necessity to change, if they are already doing it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am merely answering the hon. member's question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is not answering it. The hon. member's argument is they are doing it and have been doing it. My understanding of his argument was that he desires a change whereby the government would take over the control of the currency of the country, based on the productive capacity of the country, and issue sufficient credit to keep things moving, as it were.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: To effect exchanges.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My question is, if your tickets are based on the productive capacity of the country, you still have no power to move those who control private enterprise as it is now; they are still in a position to keep the people at poverty level and keep the government in the position where they do not have anything to issue tickets against. As I see it, you must take out of the hands of private enterprise the machinery of production so that you can work your credits and the machinery of production in coordination; you must have control over that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No. You exercise a certain amount of control over industry in this way: In the first place the power of legal tender which the government possesses enables the government to create a credit instrument which is a claim to the production of any
LMr. Blackmora.]
productive enterprise under the jurisdiction of that government. That is a principle which cannot be gainsaid. That is point No. 1. It matters not who owns the productive enterprise.
Point No. 2 is: Any industry is in business for a profit. It does not do an industry, say a coal-mining company, any good to own a coal mine if it cannot produce coal and sell it. The result is that the all-important matters to the coal business are markets and price. When the government creates a dollar bill it creates the means of buying the coal, providing a market, also the means of establishing price.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will the-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I ask hon. members not to divert me from my discussion any more at the present time. I will go into this with the greatest detail, but I should like to finish the speech I am giving and then answer questions. It is not that I have any doubt of the soundness of what I advocate-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You are thoroughly convinced yourself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Utterly, and I think by reference to the principles and practice to-day I can establish the soundness of what I have said.
I was saying that the amount of money that the government can create depends on the goods-and-services-producing-and-consum-ing-power of the country over which the government has jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is a pretty indefinite criterion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You cannot put it any other way; it is a general principle. If you had opportunity to go into details you would find it completely sound. I held that in the speech which I gave on March 8, 1938, when I moved a vote of want of confidence in the government. I merely recall that to show that our concept is permanent and stable. We have never advocated and are not advocating the creation of more money than the goods and services of the country justify; not enough to cause inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the social credit party is not against borrowing and is not against taxing and is not against private ownership, then the difference between the social credit party and the government comes down to this, just a difference in judgment as to how much money should be issued from time to time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister is coming very close to it. The first great difference between the social credit concept and the gov-

War Appropriation-Finance
ernment concept is this: social credit says that all the money in the state, all that it is possible to create, fundamentally is the property of the people in the state and should be owned by the government to be used for the welfare of the state.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
So do we. Of course the
monetary policy should be the policy that is in the interest of the welfare of the state. There is no difference between the social credit party and the government there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Only that the social credit party says that new money should be
issued as a clear asset to the state, should be a definite addition to the revenues of the state.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Even the Conservatives did that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am not saying they did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What does that mean?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Take as an illustration the $26,000,000 we talked of last night. In the last war $26,000,000 of new money was created outright by the Department of Finance, and spent, just as though it had been borrowed or as though it had been taxed. The result was the $26,000,000 was definitely added to the revenue of the country, but it was revenue which did not entail a tax on the people and did not create a debt which would go on through generations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The reason why the hon. gentleman takes that $26,000,000 is that at that time there was a gold standard, which was departed from to the extent that that $26,000,000 was created. To-day there is no gold standard, and to the extent that we borrow from the Bank of Canada, as we do to a limited extent, are we not doing exactly what that government did when it issued the $26,000,000?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think you are going into debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are not going into debt when we borrow from the Bank of Canada because we are the Bank of Canada. Therefore, the difference between the hon. gentleman and myself comes down to this, does it not, merely a matter of judgment as to how far we should go in borrowing from the Bank of Canada?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman does not say we should go the whole length. He does not say we should have borrowed $1,000,000,000 in 1940 and $2,000,000,000 in
1941 and $3,000,000,000 in 1942. He says now he does not mean that, and his party does not mean that. He believes we should go on borrowing otherwise than from the Bank of Canada, which is not borrowing at all but which is the creation of money. He says some money should be created, so the issue seems to have become just a matter of judgment as to degree. That is a very small issue, is it not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister really should be on the other side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

There is just this difference. There has been, for a considerable length of time, propaganda going out through the banks in an effort to convey to people the idea that if the government should print a one dollar bill, that is inflation. It is not inflation at all unless there is a rise in price. What we need to do all over the continent of north America in this generation is to get definitely in mind the fact that there is no inflation unless there is a rise in price, and a rise in price does not necessarily occur unless there is a shortage of goods. Once that is granted we are on a basis from which we can reason, and we will go forward during the rest of the period on that basis.
The important thing in dealing with inflation is first of all to increase your production, both in amount and in variety. The next thing is to keep your price down, perhaps by means other than price ceilings, though the price ceiling is one way of keeping prices down. Then Mr. Stewart, in a statement on June 3, points out that the coal situation in the United States is serious and that Canada depends for 60 per cent of her consumption on the United States. There is a long statement in the Ottawa Journal of May 4, to the effect that possibly coal will have to be rationed. Coal is an essential war commodity. The situation has become so serious in Britain that they have nationalized the industry and taken it over. In the face of the fuel controller making such statements, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply stressing the seriousness of the situation with respect to oil, we find in the east and in the west coal mines being closed or put on short time. The public is wondering about this.

What I should like to bring specifically to the minister's attention is this statement released from Nanaimo, British Columbia, and printed in the Canadian Tribune of this week. I am going to read it for the minister's information, because in the back of my mind for the past two years I have had the definite belief that most of the trouble we have experienced in the mining industry was organized behind the scenes by an unseen influence, and the miners have suffered the consequences:
Declaring he had uncovered a situation that was "unbelievable until he investigated," John Stokaluk, District 18 vice-president of the U.M.W.A., charged at a meeting of several hundred coal miners here that oil interests were trying to slow production in Vancouver island coal mines.
Stokaluk flew to Nanaimo following walkouts of workers in two mines. The miners' action was taken after crude unsigned pencilled notices had been posted up and Stokaluk made the direct charge that certain members of the union local were being paid to stir up trouble.
I believe that, because I have gone through similar situations.
"There is plenty of coal," he said, "but the oil interests are trying to show the people of Canada and the government that this coming winter there will be a shortage of coal and miners.
"The more strikes and shortages we have the better for the oil interests," he added.
Stokaluk told the meeting that provided the miners' legitimate grievances were properly adjusted, Vancouver island mines can supply 800.000 tons of coal a year, sufficient to meet market requirements.
Demanding immediate action to settle these legitimate grievances, he declared "that the union would fight any unpatriotic efforts, oil or other interests might make to interfere with coal production.
I know that during the past two years there have been serious upheavals in the mining industry in Nova Scotia; and, knowing that situation very well, I have time and time again come to the conclusion that interests other than the miners were the cause of 75 per cent of the trouble which has taken place since the outbreak of war. I bring this to the minister's attention specifically. I believe that the charges made by Stokaluk in Nanaimo, should be examined by this government, and examined immediately, either through the fuel control board or through someone else. If it is true that the oil interests of this country, thinking in terms of after the war, are deliberately sabotaging the coal industry and preventing its expansion at this time in order that they may build up in Canada a market for oil in the aftermath of this war, and a continuation and expansion of their own industry, it is time that we found out.
These are specific charges as carried in the public press. If they are true in respect of British Columbia, they are true of other parts of Canada. A few days ago the executive board of the miners of Nova Scotia was notified by the heads of the coal companies that from now on the mines of Nova Scotia would be on short time. It is only a few months ago that the press carried full-page statements from the same coal company, when there was an upheaval there which was not, in my opinion, organized by the men, characterizing these men as saboteurs. To-day the companies themselves are sabotaging the industry, and it is time that the people of Canada, through the medium of their responsible elected officials, came to an understanding as far as this industry is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman says that the companies are sabotaging the industry, and, he fears, at the instance of their competitors, the oil people.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think that follows.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the direct charge made by district 18 vice-president of the United Mine Workers' Association in British Columbia. He said that after investigation "he had uncovered a situation that was unbelievable", and he charged directly that the oil interests of Canada are sabotaging the mines. John Stokaluk has information of that kind at his disposal; that information should come to the government and something should be done about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I say right now that if he will forward his information, it certainly will be investigated. I am doubtful whether there is anything definite about that. On what occasion did he make his speech, or in what form?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Apparently, according to this statement, he was summoned to Nanaimo, where the mines are on short time or idle. He flew there and, addressing a mass meeting of the miners, he makes these charges. But what I am concerned about is the possibility of rationing fuel this winter. There is no oil available. The mines east and west are on short time, while the fuel controller, Mr. Stewart, is warning the people of central Canada that coal will have to be rationed. It is about time we found out why mines should be idle in such a situation.
Mr. ILSLEY; I will bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the coal administrator, and if the gentleman in Vancouver has definite information, the matter will be taken account of, if the charges and
The King's Birthday

statements are definite enough, and are based on anything except hearsay or surmise. I do not know much about the coal situation, but I am told there is a transportation bottleneck in regard to coal. That may or may not be so. I shall have to get further information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to know whether such matters as these, which affect inflation and price ceiling, may be discussed later on. Will it be in order to deal with these questions when we come to the discussion which the leader of the opposition has indicated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. I want to make it clear that the resolution about to be reported is the resolution as amended. There was a $500,000,000 reduction carried one night.
Resolution as amended reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Ilsley thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 95, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 6.16 p.m.
Monday, June 8, 1942
